title: Wystan's Unexpected Port Blossom Adventure
markdown:
Port Blossom was colour and sound, and Wystan Buttercup meant, for once, to deliver a message without becoming the entertainment.

He was an excellent scout. Knots that would hold a whale. Stars on a cloudy night. A compass true as a loyal friend. He was also, in front of everyone, a specialist in small mortifying blunders, as if a sprite timed his elbow for the most public second.

Boats bobbed, sails like captured butterflies, accordions, fried dough, salt. Bunting snapped from mast to mast. A child with a toffee-apple nearly collided with a man selling paper fish. Uniform crisp, optimism unusual, rolled message for Mayor Pumble’s announcement. Today he would shine. Today, no hitch.

Flicker the ferret occupied his shoulder, tarnished-silver fur, obsidian-bead eyes, loyalty debatable. Shiny things interested him more than Wystan’s dignity. Favourite pastime: nudging important items from pockets, as if testing destiny’s stitching.

“Right then, Flicker. Mayor Pumble. Town hall. No butterflies, no waltzes with pigeons, no inspections of picnic baskets.” Flicker twitched his nose. Wystan chose to hear comprehension.

He set off on cobbles he could read by shoe-sound: Mrs. Higgins’s shuffle, the baker’s floury patter, the fiddler’s skipping gait by the fountain. The harbour clock struck a cheerful half-hour that did not quite match the church. Paper lanterns waited for dusk in nets along the rail. A girl sold ribbons the colour of bruised plums. Wystan kept the scroll in his right hand, not the pocket Flicker preferred, and counted lamp-posts as if counting could keep a day honest. He was so inside the mission he barely saw the shadow that swooped.

A seagull of legendary size, pebble-eyes, biscuit-cracking beak, snatched the roll from his hand in a flurry of white and indignation.

“Jupiter’s jolly jellybeans.” Composure shattered. He stumbled, flailed, tripped a painter’s abandoned bucket. Yellow slapped the cobbles. The message was not eaten. It did land, damp, in a display of very expensive very blue pottery.

A woman at the stall made a sound that was not quite a scream and not quite a price. Two bowls had survived. One lid had not. Wystan groaned, retrieving soggy smudge, bowing as if bowing repaired glaze. He set a coin on the cloth without being asked; the woman looked at the coin, then at his ears, which had gone the colour of festival bunting, and decided not to add a speech. Distant delighted cackles receded. Salt and blue glaze in the nose. “Of course. A seagull. Utterly ridiculous.”

He wrung the scroll as gently as paper allows. The Mayor’s announcement had become a tide-chart of its own: words still there, edges dreaming of the harbour. Flicker descended the lamp-post in a silver slither and inspected a shard as if pricing it.

Then a sound apart from festival: a footstep like a frantic uneven dance. Thump-thump, shuffle, tap-tap-tap. New. Heading toward the market heart. Scout-sense said deliberate. Not the baker. Not Mrs. Higgins. Not the Mayor’s official roll, which Wystan knew from civic parades. This was a private rhythm wearing public cobbles.

Flicker was climbing a lamp-post with unusual agility, claws ticking metal.

“Did you see which way the bird went?” Flicker chattered at a dancer’s sequin and did not come down until the sequin turned a corner.

Wystan followed the dancing steps, message blotchy, smelling of salt and desperation. He wiped pottery dust on a handkerchief that immediately became a blue handkerchief. Past the Ferris wheel, its carriages offering slices of harbour and sky. Past children and a runaway balloon that bumped a sailor’s hat and kept going, as if it had a better appointment. A blacksmith’s clang marked time the clock would not. A stall of candied peel sweetened the air, then gave way to tar and wet rope. Near craft stalls the dance grew clearer: not drunk, not lost—making. Someone was thinking with their feet.

He ducked behind carved wooden animals, beeswax and pine. A fox with too many teeth. A whale the size of a loaf. A silver torch-beam from an organiser caught dust like brief stars. In that light: a small furry streak behind knitted scarves. Flicker.

“Traitor,” Wystan said, without heat. He pushed through wool that smelled of sheep and cinnamon. A knitter clicked disapproval and then curiosity, which in Port Blossom were often the same click.

Hunched at a rickety table, torch-flicker: a young woman, hair a tangle of artistic chaos, smock splattered, sketching with furious concentration. The frantic footsteps were hers—twitching fingers, restless making, a heel that tapped whenever a line pleased her. The damp message lay spread as a canvas. Seagulls already lived in the margins. A shard of blue pottery had been drawn larger than life, as if the glaze had opinions.

“You.”

She looked up, fawn-apologetic. “The messenger. I saw that magnificent bird snatch the scroll. So dramatic. Perfect for my series, The Perils of Port Blossom.” Seagulls, pottery shards, panicked figures. “I thought the Mayor wouldn’t mind if I borrowed it. Just to sketch.”

Wystan’s mouth hung. Borrowed. For a sketch. Between Flicker’s paws, a polished brass button from her smock. The ferret, opportunistic as always, had nudged the scroll further during the aerial assault. Not malice. Sparkle. The seagull had only added a flourish.

“So the bird, the pottery, the footsteps—it was all—”

“Artistic inspiration?” Hopeful.

He might have been angry. He found, instead, the particular tiredness of a scout who had done the job by the longest harbour route. The scroll’s ink had run at the edges, but Mayor Pumble’s looping P still stood, and the time of the announcement, and the word blossom, which the damp had tried and failed to drown.

Around them the market resumed its ordinary theatre: a woman bargaining for a carved whale, a boy dropping a marble and finding it with his ear, Flicker considering a second button and thinking better of it when Wystan coughed. The artist’s pencil hovered. “I can copy the words clean, if you like. I have a steadier hand than a seagull.”

“The Mayor likes the original mess,” Wystan said, surprising himself. “Proof of delivery.”

A booming laugh: Mayor Pumble, ear for drama, amusement instead of anger, chain of office catching the torch like a second festival. “One way to deliver a message. You arrived with a story, my boy. And you, young artist—add a touch of blue pottery.”

The stallholders who had followed the commotion waited for a scolding. Pumble gave them a parade instead. “Announcement still stands. Harbour games at dusk. And if anyone sees a seagull of unusual ambition, offer it a biscuit and a wide berth.”

Wystan handed over the battered scroll. “Mostly legible, sir.” Accomplishment not despite the chaos. Because the path had been this ridiculous and he had still walked it.

The artist offered the brass button back. Flicker looked bereaved. Wystan pocketed it for later diplomacy and left her a corner of blue glaze on a scrap of paper, since she had already drawn it anyway.

Later, fireworks in crimson and gold, he sat the quay, salt in his hair. The Ferris wheel turned like a slow constellation. Accordions found a last tune and laid it down. Somewhere a biscuit found a seagull and a truce was briefly observed. Flicker slept on his lap, button in Wystan’s pocket, blue glaze on a sleeve, uniform askew. From the town-hall steps the announcement had gone out in Pumble’s boom, slightly smudged and entirely heard. Wystan had stood at the edge of the crowd, not as entertainment, not quite as hero, only as the person who had arrived with a story the harbour already knew how to tell.

He had delivered the thing. He had named the dancing feet. The harbour lights held, and Flicker, doubtful loyalist, snored like a small motor that had decided, for one night, not to steal the plot.
characters: Wystan Buttercup (competent scout cursed with public mishaps), Flicker (a pet ferret of doubtful loyalty)
audience: children aged 11-12, high-quality story for older children
